title: Mangroves of the Indus Delta
text:
Along the creeks south of Karachi, where the Indus once poured enormous quantities of fresh water into the Arabian Sea, the grey mangrove Avicennia marina grows in conditions that would kill most trees within days. Twice a day the tide floods its roots with seawater; twice a day the water drains away, leaving mud so poor in oxygen that it smells of rotten eggs. The tree survives by dividing the work of coping among different organs.

Its first defence is at the root surface, where membranes filter out much of the salt before water enters the plant. Filtering is never perfect, however, and the salt that slips through is carried up to the leaves. There, small glands pump the excess onto the leaf surface, and on a dry afternoon the leaves of a healthy tree glitter with tiny crystals that the next breeze or shower removes. The problem of oxygen is handled separately. From the buried roots, hundreds of pencil-like shoots called pneumatophores grow upward until they stand above the mud. Their spongy tissue is dotted with pores, and at low tide air diffuses through them down to the roots below.

These adaptations are impressive, but they are not limitless. Each one costs energy, and a tree that spends heavily on pumping salt has less left over for growth. For centuries the river kept that cost manageable, because the annual flood diluted the seawater in the creeks. As more of the Indus has been diverted for irrigation upstream, the flow reaching the delta has fallen sharply in most years, and the water in parts of the creek system is now saltier than the open sea. Surveys there have found stunted stands and fewer young plants than older maps would lead one to expect.

None of this means that the mangroves are doomed. Replanting projects along the coast have restored large areas, and Avicennia is the hardiest of the local species. But it would be a mistake to read the tree's toughness as a guarantee. A plant that is merely surviving is not the same as a forest that is thriving.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The grey mangrove is the only tree able to survive in the salty, oxygen-poor creeks to the south of Karachi.
Replanting projects along the coast have now fully reversed the damage done to the delta by upstream irrigation.
Of all the mangrove's adaptations, its pneumatophores matter most, because they let the tree breathe at low tide.
The grey mangrove copes with salt and poor mud through costly adaptations, and reduced river flow is straining them.
explanation: The passage explains how the tree handles salt and low oxygen, then shows that these adaptations cost energy and are strained as less river water reaches the delta. It calls Avicennia the hardiest of the local species, so other species exist, and it says replanting has restored large areas, not that the damage is reversed.

stem: According to the passage, what happens to the salt that gets past the mangrove's roots?
options: It is stored in older leaves, which the tree then sheds.
The pneumatophores release it into the air at low tide.
Glands in the leaves push it out onto the leaf surface.
The root membranes return it to the creek on each tide.
explanation: The second paragraph says the salt that slips through is carried to the leaves, where glands pump it onto the surface as crystals. The pneumatophores are described only as channels for air, not salt.

stem: Based on the passage, a grey mangrove in a creek where river water still dilutes the seawater would most likely
options: grow better, since less of its energy would go into removing salt.
lose its pneumatophores, since it would no longer need them at all.
stop forming salt crystals on its leaves at any time of the year.
be crowded out quickly by less hardy kinds of mangrove in the area.
explanation: The third paragraph links salt-pumping to lost growth and says the river's flood once kept that cost manageable, so less salt means more energy for growth. The pneumatophores deal with oxygen, which dilution does not change, and diluted seawater is still salty, so crystals would not stop altogether.

stem: The final sentence of the passage mainly serves to
options: separate the trees' ability to endure from the health of the forest as a whole.
contradict the earlier statement that replanting projects have been successful.
suggest that Avicennia should be replaced with mangrove species that grow faster.
summarise the particular adaptations that were described in the second paragraph.
explanation: After granting that the mangroves are not doomed, the author warns that survival is not the same as health, distinguishing individual toughness from a thriving forest. The sentence does not deny the replanting success mentioned just before; it qualifies what that toughness proves.

title: Stick-Slip and the Violin Bow
text:
Rub a wet finger around the rim of a glass, push a heavy cupboard across a tiled floor, or draw a bow across a violin string, and you are listening to the same physical event. Engineers call it stick-slip motion, and it depends on a simple fact about friction: the force needed to start a surface sliding is larger than the force needed to keep it sliding.

Consider the bow. Its hair is coated with rosin, a sticky resin that makes the difference between these two forces unusually large. As the bow moves, the string at first clings to the hair and is dragged sideways with it. The string, however, is under tension, and the further it is pulled from its resting position, the harder it pulls back. At a certain point that pull exceeds the grip of the rosin, and the string breaks free. Now only the weaker sliding friction acts on it, so it flies back past the bow until, slowing at the far end of its swing, it is caught again and the cycle repeats. Each cycle lasts only a few thousandths of a second, and the regular repetition, hundreds of times per second, is what the ear hears as a note.

In the nineteenth century the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz watched bowed strings through a vibrating microscope and found that their motion was not the smooth curve people had assumed but a sharp corner racing back and forth along the string. His work helped explain why bowing technique matters so much. If the player presses too lightly, the string slips before it has been carried far enough, and the tone turns thin and airy; press too hard and the string is held too long, producing a harsh scratch. Between these limits lies a range of pressures that shifts with the speed of the bow and its distance from the bridge, which is why beginners take months to find it.

What sounds like music in a concert hall is a nuisance elsewhere. The squeal of car brakes and the groan of a door hinge are also stick-slip, and much of the effort in designing such parts goes into making the two kinds of friction as nearly equal as possible.

stem: The main purpose of the passage is to
options: explain a kind of friction, using the bowed violin string as its main example.
argue that the violin is harder to learn than any other string instrument.
describe how Helmholtz designed and built a new kind of vibrating microscope.
propose several practical ways for engineers to make car brakes quieter.
explanation: The passage defines stick-slip motion, walks through it in detail with the bow, and closes with other examples of the same effect. Brakes and the difficulty of learning appear only as supporting details, and the passage says Helmholtz used the microscope, not that he built it.

stem: According to the passage, the rosin on a bow's hair
options: lowers the tension in the string so that the string can vibrate more freely.
widens the gap between the force that starts sliding and the force that keeps it going.
protects the hair from wearing out after many hours of regular playing.
stops the string from ever slipping past the hair while the bow moves.
explanation: The second paragraph says rosin makes the difference between the starting and sliding forces unusually large. It does not stop slipping altogether; the string breaks free in every cycle, which is how the note is made.

stem: Based on the passage, which change would most likely make a squealing door hinge quieter?
options: Making the friction that starts motion closer to the friction during motion
Coating the hinge with a sticky resin like rosin to increase its grip
Making the door heavier so that it swings open more slowly each time
Opening the door faster so that each stick-slip cycle is shorter
explanation: The last paragraph says designers fight squeals by making the two kinds of friction nearly equal, since stick-slip depends on the gap between them. A rosin-like coating would widen that gap and make the squeal worse.

stem: The passage presents Helmholtz's observation mainly as
options: evidence that a bowed string moves in the smooth curve that players must control.
a finding that corrected an earlier assumption and showed why technique matters.
a historical curiosity with little bearing on how players are taught today.
proof that the rosin on a bow wears away at a steady rate during each note.
explanation: Helmholtz found a sharp corner rather than the smooth curve people had assumed, and the passage says his work helped explain why bowing pressure matters. The smooth curve is the assumption he overturned, so the option built on it reverses the passage.

title: Drilled Teeth at Mehrgarh
text:
When archaeologists began digging at Mehrgarh, at the foot of the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, in the 1970s, they expected to learn about early farming. The site did not disappoint: its lowest layers, laid down more than 8,000 years ago, hold some of the earliest evidence in South Asia of people growing barley and herding goats and cattle. Decades later, however, the site produced a discovery that no one had been looking for, and it came not from the fields but from the mouths of the dead.

While examining teeth from the settlement's graveyard under a microscope, researchers noticed small, neat holes in several molars. The holes were round, a few millimetres deep and too regular to be cavities caused by decay. Their walls bore faint circular grooves, the kind of marks a rotating tool leaves behind. Because the people of Mehrgarh were skilled bead-makers who used bow-driven flint drills to pierce stones, the researchers proposed that the same technology had been turned on human teeth. In other words, someone had been drilling living patients.

Two further details strengthened that reading. First, the holes were found on teeth at the back of the mouth, where they could not have served as decoration. Second, the edges of some holes were smoothed by chewing, which could only have happened if the person went on eating for some time after the work was done. Several holes also matched places where decay had begun, though the researchers were careful to say that the purpose of the treatment could not be proved.

What makes the find puzzling is its brevity. The drilled teeth come from a span of roughly 1,500 years, and in the later graves the practice disappears. Perhaps it was abandoned because it did little to relieve pain; perhaps it continued in a form that left no trace once the tools changed. The evidence cannot settle the matter. What it does show is that the line between craft and medicine was thinner than we tend to assume: the same hands that shaped beads for trade may also have reached, carefully, into a neighbour's mouth.

stem: Which choice best summarises the passage?
options: Mehrgarh matters mainly because it shows where farming first began anywhere in the world.
The bead-makers of Mehrgarh traded their flint drills with communities across South Asia.
Researchers have proved that the people of Mehrgarh drilled teeth in order to treat decay.
Drilled molars from Mehrgarh point to an early form of dentistry that later disappeared.
explanation: Most of the passage describes the drilled teeth, the evidence that they were treated in living people, and the puzzle of why the practice ended. The researchers explicitly say the purpose could not be proved, so the claim that they proved it overstates the evidence.

options: contained traces of a filling material.
showed circular grooves from a drill.
were found only in bead-makers' graves.
were on teeth at the back of the mouth.
explanation: The third paragraph says the holes were at the back of the mouth, where they could not have served as decoration. The grooves are real evidence, but they show that a rotating tool was used, not that the holes were not ornamental.

stem: The passage indicates that the smoothing of some holes' edges by chewing shows that
options: the drilling must have been carried out after the person had died.
at least some people lived on and used the tooth after it was drilled.
the people of Mehrgarh ate an unusually coarse and gritty diet.
the holes were first made by decay and only later by a tool.
explanation: Chewing could smooth the edges only if the person kept eating after the work was done, so some patients survived the procedure. That same reasoning rules out drilling after death.

stem: In the final paragraph, the author's attitude toward explanations for the end of the practice is best described as
options: confident that it ended because it failed to relieve any pain.
dismissive of the idea that the tools of Mehrgarh ever changed.
critical of researchers for neglecting the settlement's later graves.
tentative, since the evidence cannot decide between possibilities.
explanation: The author offers two possibilities with "Perhaps" and then states that the evidence cannot settle the matter. The pain explanation is only one of the options raised, not a conclusion the author commits to.

title: When Clocks Agreed
text:
Before the railways, every town kept its own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the local church or town hall, and because the sun moves westward, noon in Bristol arrived roughly ten minutes after noon in London. For most of history the difference did not matter. A traveller on horseback could not cover the distance fast enough to notice, and a clock that disagreed with a neighbouring town's was simply one more local custom, like a dialect or a market day.

The railway changed that by making speed and coordination matter at once. A timetable is a promise that a train will be at a given place at a given minute, and a promise of that kind needs a single clock behind it. In Britain, the Great Western Railway began running its trains on London time in 1840, and other companies soon followed. Stations displayed the railway's time, sometimes alongside the local time, and a few public clocks were built with two minute hands to show both. Passengers grumbled, and some towns held out for years, but the advantage of a shared standard kept growing as lines multiplied and the telegraph made it possible to send a time signal from Greenwich across the country in an instant. By the time Parliament made Greenwich time the legal standard in 1880, much of the country had long since adopted it in practice.

North America faced the same problem on a far larger scale, with dozens of railway times in use at once. In 1883 the railways there agreed among themselves to divide the continent into broad zones, each an hour apart, and most cities adjusted their clocks on the appointed day. A year later, an international conference in Washington chose the meridian through Greenwich as the starting line for the world's longitude.

It is tempting to tell this story as a victory of science over superstition. That account misses the point. Local solar time was not wrong; it was perfectly accurate for a world that moved slowly. What the railways created was not a truer time but a more useful one, and people accepted it because the price of disagreement had become too high to pay.

stem: Which choice best states the central claim of the passage?
options: Standard time spread because railways needed coordination, not because local time was inaccurate.
Local solar time was a superstition that science gradually replaced during the nineteenth century.
North American railways adopted standard time earlier and more smoothly than British ones did.
The telegraph, more than the railway, was the main reason towns gave up keeping their own time.
explanation: The final paragraph states the claim directly: local time was accurate, and the railways made a more useful time, not a truer one. The author names the science-over-superstition story only to reject it.

stem: According to the passage, what happened in Britain in 1880?
options: A railway first ran its trains on London time.
Greenwich time became the legal standard.
A conference chose the Greenwich meridian.
The telegraph first carried a time signal.
explanation: The second paragraph says Parliament made Greenwich time the legal standard in 1880. The Great Western Railway's switch came in 1840, and the meridian conference was held in Washington in 1884.

stem: The passage suggests that some public clocks had two minute hands mainly because
options: the law required every town in Britain to display London time from 1840.
clockmakers of the period could not keep a single minute hand accurate.
travellers wished to compare British time with the time in North America.
local time and railway time were both in use while towns made the change.
explanation: The clocks showed both the railway's time and local time, which makes sense only while the two were in use side by side during the transition. The legal standard came in 1880, so no law forced towns to show London time in 1840.

stem: The author mentions "a victory of science over superstition" in order to
options: support the view that local solar time rested on mistaken popular beliefs.
show that scientists opposed the railways' choice of a single standard time.
explain why a number of towns resisted railway time for so many years.
introduce a reading of the history that the author then goes on to reject.
explanation: The phrase is followed at once by "That account misses the point" and by the claim that local solar time was not wrong. The author raises the view in order to dismiss it, so it cannot be support for that view.

title: Why Recall Beats Rereading
text:
Ask a student how she prepares for an examination, and the answer is often some version of reading: going over notes, highlighting the textbook, rereading chapters until they feel familiar. The method is popular because it feels productive. Each pass through the material is smoother than the last, and that growing ease is easily mistaken for learning. A large body of research suggests the feeling is misleading.

In a typical experiment, two groups study the same passage once. One group then reads it three more times; the other reads it once more and spends the remaining time trying to write down everything it can remember, without looking. Tested five minutes later, the rereaders usually do slightly better. Tested a week later, the pattern reverses, and the group that practised recalling often remembers substantially more. Psychologists call this the testing effect, though the name is somewhat misleading, since the benefit comes not from being graded but from the effort of pulling information out of memory.

Why should retrieval help? One explanation is that each successful act of recall strengthens the route to a memory, much as walking a path through a field keeps it clear. Another is that retrieval reveals gaps. A student who rereads a definition recognises it and moves on; a student who tries to state it from memory discovers that she cannot, and knows exactly what to study next.

The awkward part is that retrieval practice feels worse. Struggling to remember is uncomfortable, and in surveys learners who used it often rate it as less effective than rereading, even after their own scores have shown the opposite. Some researchers describe such methods as "desirable difficulties": conditions that slow learning down in the moment but make it last.

None of this means rereading is useless. A first reading is necessary to have something to retrieve, and a confused student may need to return to the text. The point is about proportion. A teacher in Peshawar who ends each lesson with three quick questions, answered from memory and not marked, may be doing more for her pupils' examination results than another hour of revision ever could.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Rereading is a useless way to study, and students should replace it entirely with tests that are graded.
Recalling material from memory builds longer-lasting learning than rereading, though it feels less effective.
Students learn best when every lesson ends with a short written examination that the teacher marks.
Rereading gives better results than practising recall when students are tested just a few minutes after study.
explanation: The passage argues that retrieval practice produces more durable learning even though learners judge it less effective. Rereading does win on an immediate test, but that is one detail of the experiment, and the author says the benefit lasts a week, not five minutes.

stem: According to the passage, in the typical experiment the group that practised recalling
options: did better than the rereaders on both the early and the later test.
read the passage four times in all before it was finally tested.
did slightly worse after five minutes but better a week later.
was graded on its recall, which made its members work harder.
explanation: The second paragraph says the rereaders usually do slightly better after five minutes and that the pattern reverses after a week. The author stresses that the benefit does not come from being graded.

stem: The survey results described in the fourth paragraph suggest that learners
options: come to prefer retrieval practice once they see their improved scores.
remember more when they are free to choose their own way of studying.
may not be reliable judges of which study methods help them most.
find rereading uncomfortable because it exposes the gaps in what they know.
explanation: Learners rated retrieval as less effective even after their own scores showed it worked better, so their sense of what helps is unreliable. That same finding rules out the idea that they switch preference once they see the scores.

stem: As used in the final paragraph, "proportion" most nearly means
options: balance
symmetry
dimension
fairness
explanation: The author has just granted that rereading has a place, so "proportion" refers to the balance between rereading and recall in a student's time. Symmetry and dimension describe shape or size, which do not fit a point about how study time is shared.

title: A Capital Drawn in Advance
text:
Most capital cities grew for centuries before anyone tried to plan them. Islamabad was planned before it grew. When Pakistan's government decided at the end of the 1950s to build a new capital at the foot of the Margalla Hills, it hired the Greek planner Constantinos Doxiadis, whose firm produced a master plan in 1960. The city that resulted still shows his ideas more clearly than almost any other city shows its designer's.

Doxiadis distrusted the traditional city that spreads outward in rings from a central core. As such a city grows, he argued, its centre becomes choked, because every new suburb adds traffic heading for the same few streets. His alternative, which he called the dynapolis, or dynamic city, was meant to grow in one main direction along a widening band, so that the centre could move forward with the city instead of being smothered by it.

The building block of this plan was the sector. Islamabad's sectors, each roughly two kilometres on a side and identified by a letter and a number such as F-7 or G-9, were laid out on a grid separated by broad avenues. Each sector was intended to be a largely self-sufficient community, divided into smaller sub-sectors and served by its own central market, the markaz, together with schools, mosques and green spaces within walking distance. Through traffic would stay on the avenues, leaving the interior streets quiet.

Much of this worked as intended. Visitors still remark on Islamabad's greenery and its orderly addresses, and the markaz remains the everyday heart of each neighbourhood. Yet the plan had a weakness that only time could reveal. It assumed that growth could be steered by drawing lines on a map. In practice, people who could not afford the planned sectors, including many of the workers who built them, settled wherever land was available, and informal settlements appeared on the city's edges and along its streams. The tidy grid, in other words, could organise the city that was planned, but it had no place for the city that actually arrived.

stem: The passage is mainly concerned with
options: comparing Islamabad with older capital cities that grew without any plan.
arguing that informal settlements should be cleared from Islamabad's edges.
explaining why the Margalla Hills were chosen as the site of the capital.
describing the ideas behind Islamabad's plan and where they fell short.
explanation: The passage sets out Doxiadis's dynapolis and sector ideas, notes what worked, and ends with the plan's blind spot. Older unplanned capitals appear only in the opening contrast, and the author describes informal settlements without recommending their removal.

stem: According to the passage, the broad avenues between sectors were meant to
options: mark the outer limits of each sector's central market and its shops.
allow the centre of the city to move forward as the city grew larger.
carry through traffic so that streets inside the sectors stayed quiet.
provide green spaces within easy walking distance of every household.
explanation: The third paragraph says through traffic would stay on the avenues, leaving the interior streets quiet. A moving centre is the purpose of the dynapolis as a whole, not of the avenues.

stem: Based on the passage, Doxiadis would most likely have criticised a city in which
options: each neighbourhood has its own market that residents can reach on foot.
homes are identified by letters and numbers that follow a regular grid pattern.
growth takes place mainly in one direction along a band that keeps widening.
all new suburbs depend on roads that lead to one fixed central district.
explanation: Doxiadis argued that a city growing in rings from one core chokes its centre because every new suburb sends traffic to the same streets. Growth in one direction along a widening band is his own dynapolis, so he would have approved of it.

options: the people and settlements that the plan made no provision for.
the visitors who still admire Islamabad's greenery and addresses.
the sectors that were completed exactly as the master plan required.
the government offices that moved to the foot of the Margalla Hills.
explanation: The sentence contrasts the planned city with the residents who could not afford the sectors and settled informally, which the grid had no place for. The visitors are mentioned earlier as evidence that parts of the plan succeeded.

title: The Tanpura's Drone
text:
In a performance of Hindustani classical music, the instrument that plays the most notes is rarely the one that matters most. Behind the singer, often played by a student who sits almost motionless for an hour, is the tanpura: a long-necked lute with four strings that are never pressed against the neck and never play a melody. The player simply plucks the open strings one after another, in a slow, unchanging cycle. To a listener new to the tradition, it can sound like nothing more than a background hum.

That hum does a great deal of work. Its strings are usually tuned to the tonic, the home note of the raga, and to one other note, most often the fifth, so the drone sets out the frame within which every other note is heard. A raga is defined less by a fixed scale than by the relationship of each note to the tonic, and a singer judges whether a note is in tune by how it sits against the drone. Without the tanpura, small drifts in pitch can pass unnoticed; with it, they become obvious, almost painful.

The instrument's distinctive shimmer comes from its bridge. Instead of touching the string at a single sharp point, as on a guitar, the string lies across a broad, gently curved surface of bone or wood. The effect, known as jawari, depends on a cotton thread slipped under each string to adjust exactly where it grazes the bridge. As the string vibrates, it repeatedly brushes against this curve, and the contact constantly reshapes its motion, releasing a cascade of high overtones that rise and fade during each note. Moving the thread by a fraction of a millimetre can turn a dull tone into a ringing one, and skilled makers guard their methods carefully.

Electronic drone boxes and mobile apps now offer a cheaper and more portable alternative, and many students practise with them. Many performers, however, still insist on the real instrument. Its sound, they say, is never quite the same from one cycle to the next, and that slight restlessness gives the singer something living to sing against.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The tanpura is the hardest instrument in Hindustani music to master and takes many years of training.
Electronic drones have now replaced the tanpura in most concerts of Hindustani classical music.
Although it plays no melody, the tanpura gives the music its pitch frame and a distinctive sound.
A raga is defined by a fixed scale, which the tanpura plays through before the singer begins.
explanation: The passage explains how the drone sets the frame for judging pitch and how the bridge creates its shimmer. It says the player sits almost motionless plucking open strings, and that a raga is defined less by a fixed scale than by each note's relation to the tonic.

stem: According to the passage, the cotton thread under each string is used to
options: set precisely where the string grazes the curved bridge.
stop the string from touching the bridge as it vibrates.
tune the string to the tonic or to the fifth of the raga.
keep the string from being pressed against the long neck.
explanation: The third paragraph says the thread adjusts exactly where the string grazes the bridge. The jawari effect depends on the string brushing against the bridge, so stopping that contact would remove the shimmer.

stem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the second paragraph that a singer performing without any drone would be
options: unable to perform a raga, because a raga is defined by a drone.
more likely to choose a raga that is built on a simple fixed scale.
less likely to notice when her notes drift slightly off pitch.
obliged to pluck the tonic herself on a second stringed instrument.
explanation: The paragraph says small drifts in pitch can pass unnoticed without the tanpura but become obvious with it. A raga is defined by each note's relation to the tonic, not by the drone itself, so the singer could still perform, only with less control.

stem: The final paragraph mainly serves to
options: note a modern substitute and give performers' reason for still preferring the original.
argue that students who practise with apps can never become skilled concert performers.
describe how instrument makers protect their methods for adjusting the bridge.
show that the tanpura's sound changes from cycle to cycle because it is poorly made.
explanation: The paragraph mentions drone boxes and apps, then reports that many performers prefer the real tanpura because its slight variation sounds alive. It says many students practise with apps without judging their future skill, and it treats the variation as a strength, not a defect.

title: Neptune, Vulcan and the Failed Prediction
text:
In 1846 the French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier did something that seemed close to magic. Uranus, then the most distant known planet, had been drifting slightly from the path that Newton's laws predicted. Rather than conclude that the laws were wrong, Le Verrier assumed that an unseen planet was pulling on Uranus, and he calculated where it must be. He sent his prediction to the Berlin Observatory, and on the very night the letter arrived, an astronomer there found Neptune within about a degree of the predicted spot. It was celebrated as one of the great triumphs of science.

Some years later Le Verrier turned to a similar problem. Mercury's orbit also departed slightly from Newtonian predictions: the point at which the planet comes closest to the sun shifts a little more each century than the pull of the known planets could explain. The method that had found Neptune suggested an answer, and Le Verrier proposed an undiscovered planet orbiting even closer to the sun. It was given a name, Vulcan, and for decades astronomers searched for it, particularly during solar eclipses, when the sun's glare is blocked. Several reported sightings. None was confirmed. The puzzle was finally solved in 1915, not by a new planet but by a new theory of gravity: Einstein's general relativity accounted for Mercury's motion with no extra planet required.

The two episodes are often told separately, one as a success and one as an embarrassment, but placed side by side they raise a hard question for anyone who thinks science advances simply by rejecting theories that fail their tests. In both cases a theory made a prediction that observation contradicted. In the first, defending the theory by adding an unseen object was exactly the right move; in the second, it was exactly the wrong one. At the time, nobody could have known which was which. A failed prediction tells us that something in our reasoning is mistaken, but not, by itself, which part.

This does not make scientific judgment arbitrary. The Vulcan hypothesis was eventually abandoned because repeated searches found nothing. But it does suggest that the line between sensibly protecting a good theory and stubbornly refusing to give up a bad one is often drawn clearly only in hindsight.

stem: Which choice best states the central claim of the passage?
options: The case of Vulcan shows that Newton's laws were never as reliable as nineteenth-century scientists believed.
A failed prediction does not show which assumption is at fault, so the right response is often clear only later.
Scientists should always reject a theory as soon as observation contradicts one of its predictions.
Discoveries such as that of Neptune usually owe more to good luck than to careful calculation.
explanation: The third and fourth paragraphs draw the lesson from the paired stories: a contradicted prediction signals an error somewhere but not where, and the difference between wise defence and stubbornness often appears only in hindsight. The passage questions, rather than recommends, rejecting a theory at the first failed test.

stem: According to the passage, astronomers looked for Vulcan especially during solar eclipses because
options: the sun's glare was blocked at those times.
Mercury was closest to the sun at those times.
Le Verrier had said an eclipse would reveal it.
Einstein's theory said it would be visible then.
explanation: The second paragraph says the searches were made particularly during eclipses, when the sun's glare is blocked. Einstein's theory removed the need for Vulcan altogether, so it predicted no such sighting.

stem: The passage suggests that the reported sightings of Vulcan were
options: what persuaded Einstein to develop his new theory of gravity in 1915.
eventually confirmed by astronomers working at the Berlin Observatory.
evidence that Neptune itself had been found by chance, not calculation.
mistaken, since no extra planet was needed to explain Mercury's orbit.
explanation: None of the sightings was confirmed, and general relativity explained Mercury's motion with no extra planet, so the reports must have been errors. The passage gives no link between the sightings and Einstein's work.

options: criticise Le Verrier for proposing Vulcan without enough supporting evidence.

title: The Neighbourhood Committee
text:
In much of Pakistan, a family that wants to buy a refrigerator, pay a daughter's university fees or restock a small shop may not go to a bank at all. Instead it joins a committee. Ten neighbours, say, each agree to pay Rs 10,000 into a common pot every month. Each month one member, chosen by lot or by agreement, takes the whole Rs 100,000, and the cycle continues until everyone has had a turn. Economists call such arrangements rotating savings and credit associations, and versions of them exist on every continent, from the tanda of Mexico to the susu of West Africa.

At first glance the committee seems pointless. No interest is paid, and the total each member receives is exactly what she puts in. Why not simply save Rs 10,000 a month at home? The answer becomes clear if one looks at timing. Saving alone, a member would have Rs 100,000 only at the end of ten months. In a committee, every member except the last receives it sooner, and the first receives it immediately. For all but one participant, then, the committee works like an interest-free loan, repaid in monthly instalments.

Even the last member gains something, and here economics meets psychology. Money kept at home is easy to spend: a wedding, a broken motorcycle or a relative's request can swallow it. A monthly payment owed to neighbours is far harder to skip. Researchers who study such groups describe the committee as a commitment device, a way for people to bind their future selves to a plan they already know they want.

The system's strength, however, is also its risk. It rests entirely on trust and social pressure, and little but reputation prevents a member who has already collected the pot from disappearing. That is why committees are usually formed among relatives, colleagues or long-standing neighbours, and why an organiser with a reputation to protect is often at the centre of one. Where those bonds are weak, the arrangement can collapse, leaving the members still waiting for their turn with payments made and nothing received.

explanation: The passage poses the puzzle of an arrangement that pays no interest and answers it with timing and commitment. It does mention the risk of collapse, but only where trust is weak, not as a general warning against committees.

explanation: Every member except the last collects Rs 100,000 before contributing that amount, then pays it back in monthly instalments. The passage mentions no extra payments from the organiser, and each member pays the same Rs 10,000 a month.

title: The Radio in the Storeroom
text:
The radio had been silent for eleven years when Sana carried it down from the storeroom. It was her grandfather's, a wooden cabinet the size of a small suitcase, with a dial that still showed the names of cities he had listened to as a young man: Delhi, Kabul, Colombo, Cairo. Since his death it had stood under a sheet beside the old trunks, and no one had thought of it except as furniture.

She had not meant to repair it. Her physics teacher in Multan had asked the class to take apart something electrical and explain how it worked, and the radio was the only thing in the house no one would miss. But when she unscrewed the back panel and saw the valves standing in their sockets like small glass towers, she found she wanted, very much, to hear it again.

It took most of the winter. Her uncle, who had once sold electrical goods in Hussain Agahi bazaar, told her which parts were likely to fail, and a shopkeeper there found her two replacement valves in a box he had not opened in years. She learned to test a capacitor, to trace a wire from the dial to the tuning coil, to smell the difference between dust warming up and insulation beginning to burn. Twice she switched it on and heard nothing. Once she heard a loud crack and switched it off again quickly.

On the evening it finally worked, the family was in the courtyard. At first there was only a low hiss, and then, as she turned the dial slowly, a voice emerged reading the news, faint and wavering, from somewhere far beyond the city. Her grandmother, who had said little all winter, put down her tea.

"He used to turn it exactly like that," she said. "Slowly, as if the station might run away."

Sana kept her hand on the dial. She had written twelve pages on resistance and frequency for her teacher, and every word of them was correct. None of them, she thought, had been about this.

title: Lichens and the Air
text:
On an old gravestone, a rooftop or the bark of a roadside tree, a lichen looks like a single plain organism: a crust of grey, orange or pale green that seems hardly alive. In fact it is a partnership. Every lichen consists of a fungus living together with a partner that can photosynthesise, either a green alga or a cyanobacterium. The fungus provides the structure, a tough body that holds water and anchors the lichen to its surface; the partner, sheltered inside, uses sunlight to make sugars that feed them both. The arrangement is so successful that lichens grow on bare rock in deserts and on the edges of polar ice, places where neither partner could survive alone.

That same arrangement makes lichens unusually sensitive to the air. Unlike a flowering plant, a lichen has no roots and no waxy coating to control what enters it. It takes in water and minerals directly from rain, mist and dust, absorbing whatever they carry. When the air contains sulphur dioxide, a gas released by burning coal and some kinds of fuel oil, the lichen absorbs it too, and the delicate photosynthetic partner is damaged first. Because many lichens grow slowly, often only a few millimetres a year, they cannot quickly recover.

Naturalists noticed the consequences long before they understood the chemistry. In nineteenth-century Europe, observers recorded that lichens were vanishing from the trees of industrial cities while still flourishing in the countryside nearby. Later researchers turned the observation into a tool. Different species tolerate different levels of pollution, so a survey of which lichens grow on the trees of a district works as a rough, inexpensive record of its air quality over many years, something a single reading from an instrument cannot provide.

The story has had a hopeful turn. In several cities where coal burning has declined, lichens have returned to trees on which none had been seen for generations. Their return is not proof that the air is clean, since lichens respond more strongly to some pollutants than to others. But it is a reminder that some of the most useful scientific instruments are alive.

title: Why Ice Is Slippery
text:
Everyone knows that ice is slippery, but for more than a century and a half physicists have disagreed about why. The question sounds simple, since a smooth, hard surface might be expected to offer little grip. Yet glass is smooth and hard too, and a person in ordinary shoes can walk across a polished glass floor without falling. Something about ice is different.

The explanation found in many textbooks is pressure melting. Ice is unusual in that its melting point falls slightly when it is squeezed, so the weight of a skater, concentrated on a thin blade, was thought to melt a film of water beneath it. The skater, on this view, glides on water rather than on ice. The idea is neat, but the numbers do not support it. Even the narrow blade of a skate lowers the melting point by only a degree or so, and people slip on ice that is far colder than that, at temperatures where pressure alone could never produce liquid water.

A second explanation is frictional heating: the rubbing of a moving shoe or blade warms the surface enough to melt a thin layer. This certainly happens once sliding has begun, but it cannot explain why a person standing still on ice may begin to slip in the first place.

The most promising answer goes back to an idea Michael Faraday proposed in the 1850s. Faraday suggested that the surface of ice is covered, even well below freezing, by an extremely thin layer that behaves partly like a liquid. Molecules at the surface have fewer neighbours to hold them in place than those inside the crystal, so they are less firmly locked into its structure. Modern experiments have detected such a layer, only a few molecules thick, and computer simulations reproduce it. Many researchers now think this layer, perhaps combined with frictional heating, accounts for most of ice's slipperiness, though they still argue over how the layer behaves under a moving foot.

The case is a useful reminder that a familiar explanation can survive for generations simply because no one checks the arithmetic.

explanation: The passage examines pressure melting, frictional heating and Faraday's surface layer in turn and judges how well each works. Skating appears only as an example, and the passage credits modern experiments, not Faraday, with detecting the layer.

title: Reading the Rings
text:
A tree in a temperate forest adds a new ring of wood every year, and the width of that ring depends on the weather: a wet, mild year produces a broad ring, a year of drought a narrow one. Taken alone, a single tree's rings tell us little more than its age. Taken together, the rings of many trees tell us something far more useful, because trees growing in the same region respond to the same weather and therefore record the same sequence of broad and narrow years.

This shared pattern is the basis of dendrochronology, or tree-ring dating. Researchers begin with living trees, whose outermost ring can be assigned to the current year, and count backwards. They then look for older timbers, such as beams from old houses or logs preserved in bogs, whose inner rings overlap with the outer rings of the living trees. Where the patterns match, the two sequences can be joined, and the record extends further back. Step by step, by linking overlapping pieces, researchers in several parts of the world have built continuous chronologies stretching back thousands of years.

The method's great strength is its precision. Radiocarbon dating can usually place a sample only within a range of decades, but a timber that matches a master chronology can be dated to a single year, and if its outermost ring beneath the bark survives, sometimes to a single season. Archaeologists have used this to show, for instance, that the beams of a medieval roof were all cut in the same winter, or that a building thought to be ancient was in fact largely rebuilt centuries later.

The method also has limits. It works only where trees lay down distinct annual rings, which rules out many tropical forests where growth continues all year. A sample must contain enough rings for a reliable match; a short fragment may fit several places in a chronology equally well. And the date obtained is the year the tree died, not the year the wood was used. A beam salvaged from an older building and reused, a common practice where good timber was scarce, can make a structure appear older than it is. The tree remembers its own life precisely; what people later did with it, the rings cannot say.

explanation: The passage explains how overlapping ring patterns are linked, praises the method's precision and then sets out its limits. It compares the method with radiocarbon dating but never says one has replaced the other, and it says tropical trees often lack distinct rings.

title: Setting Nastaliq in Type
text:
For most of the twentieth century, a page of an Urdu newspaper was written by hand. In the offices of the large dailies, rows of professional calligraphers, known as katibs, copied out each day's news in the Nastaliq style, and their pages were photographed and printed. The method was slow and expensive, and a paper's look depended on the skill and stamina of its writers. Yet attempts to replace them with metal type had repeatedly disappointed readers.

The difficulty lay in the script itself. In Nastaliq, the letters of a word do not sit on a single straight line, as they do in the simpler Naskh style used for much printed Arabic. Each word slopes downward from right to left, and a letter changes its shape according to the letters on either side of it, sometimes dramatically. Type founders had dealt with this by making separate pieces for each form of each letter and setting them side by side, but the joins never looked natural, and many readers found such pages stiff and hard to read. Some publishers switched to Naskh; most Urdu newspapers kept their katibs.

The solution, when it came in the early 1980s, reversed the usual approach. Ahmed Mirza Jamil, a Pakistani calligrapher and artist, working with the British typesetting firm Monotype, did not try to build words from individual letters. Instead he wrote out thousands of complete letter combinations, or ligatures, by hand, and these were stored in the computer so that a word could be assembled from a few whole, correctly joined units. The result, called Noori Nastaliq, looked like the work of a skilled katib because, in a sense, it was.

The newspaper Jang was among the first to adopt the system, and within a few years computer typesetting had spread across the Urdu press. Something was lost: the profession of the newspaper katib declined sharply, and with it a great deal of everyday craftsmanship. But the readers whose habits had defeated decades of metal type were finally satisfied. A technology had succeeded, for once, by adapting itself to the script rather than asking the script to adapt.

explanation: The passage explains why Nastaliq resisted metal type and how Noori Nastaliq solved the problem. It says only some publishers switched to Naskh while most newspapers kept their katibs, and Jang appears only as an early adopter.

title: When Rewards Backfire
text:
Economists have a name for a reward that produces the opposite of what it was meant to: a perverse incentive. The examples are often funny in hindsight. A city troubled by rats offers a payment for every rat tail handed in, and residents begin breeding rats. A factory pays workers by the number of items they finish, and quality falls. A hospital is judged by how quickly it treats patients in its emergency ward, and some patients are left waiting in ambulances outside, where the clock has not yet started.

The common thread is that the people who design a reward usually care about one thing but can measure only another. The city wants fewer rats but can count only tails. The hospital wants patients treated promptly but can record only the time between arrival in the ward and first attention. As long as the measured thing and the desired thing move together, the reward works. Once people discover that they can move the measure without moving the goal, the two come apart, and the reward begins to pay for the wrong behaviour.

This is not usually a story about dishonesty. Most of the people who respond to a perverse incentive are doing what they were, in effect, told to do. A teacher whose salary depends on her pupils' scores in a single examination is not cheating if she spends the term drilling them in that examination's format; she is responding sensibly to the signal she has been sent. The fault lies less with her than with a system that treated one narrow number as if it captured everything it valued.

What can designers do? One response is to measure several things at once, so that improving one at the expense of the others brings no reward. Another is to change measures from time to time, before people learn to game them. A third, harder to put into practice, is to rely partly on judgment: to ask experienced people to assess whether the real goal is being met. None of these is perfect. But each begins from the same recognition, that a number is a tool for seeing a goal, not the goal itself.

title: The Curse of Knowledge
text:
In a simple classroom experiment, one student is asked to tap out the rhythm of a well-known song on a desk, and a second student must guess the song. Before starting, the tapper is asked to predict how often listeners will succeed. Tappers typically expect listeners to guess correctly about half the time. In practice, listeners rarely manage more than a handful of correct guesses in every hundred tries.

The gap is not explained by poor tapping. The difficulty is that the tapper hears the song. As she taps, the melody plays in her head, and the taps seem to her to carry it clearly. The listener hears only a series of knocks, which could belong to almost any tune. Once we know something, it becomes strangely hard to imagine not knowing it, and we judge what others will understand by what we ourselves perceive. Psychologists call this the curse of knowledge.

The effect has been found far beyond the classroom. Experts who write instructions skip steps that seem too obvious to mention. Engineers design controls that are perfectly clear to the people who built them and baffling to everyone else. A senior doctor explaining a diagnosis may use a word that she has used every day for twenty years and forget that the patient has never heard it. In each case, the problem is not a lack of knowledge but an excess of it, combined with an inability to set it aside.

Simply telling people about the bias does surprisingly little to reduce it. In several studies, participants who were warned about the effect still overestimated how much others would understand. What helps more is direct contact with a real beginner: watching someone struggle with the instructions, or asking a listener to explain back what she has heard. Such experiences force the expert to see the gap rather than merely to accept that it exists.

There is an irony here for anyone who teaches. The better a teacher knows a subject, the more vulnerable she may be to forgetting how difficult it once seemed, which is perhaps why the most helpful explanation of a hard idea sometimes comes from a classmate who understood it only yesterday.

explanation: The tapping experiment and the later examples all show knowers overestimating what others will understand. The fourth paragraph says warnings do surprisingly little, so they are not the best remedy.

title: The Letter-Writer of Rawalpindi
text:
Every morning at eight, Rahim Bakhsh unfolded his table under the neem tree outside the general post office in Rawalpindi, set out an inkpot, a pad of blue airmail paper and a tin of envelopes, and waited. For forty years people had come to him with things they could not write themselves: a son's request for money from Dubai answered, a complaint to the electricity board, a proposal of marriage phrased so that refusal would embarrass no one.

He had learned early that his customers rarely knew what they wanted to say. A farmer would ask for a letter telling his brother the harvest was poor, and after ten minutes of talk it would emerge that what he really wanted was to ask forgiveness for a quarrel three years old. Rahim Bakhsh wrote both. He wrote the harvest first, because that was what the farmer had asked for, and the forgiveness last, in a single sentence, so that the brother could pretend not to have noticed it if he chose.

Lately the customers were fewer. Young men who once would have queued at his table now typed messages on their phones while walking past him. His nephew had offered, more than once, to find him a job in a shop with a fan and a chair that did not wobble.

That afternoon a girl of perhaps nineteen sat down across from him. She had a phone in her hand, and she explained, a little embarrassed, that she could send her grandmother in Gujrat a message in a second. But her grandmother could not read, and the neighbour who read things aloud to her would read out whatever came, exactly as it was written. "I want her to hear it the way you write," the girl said. "Properly."

Rahim Bakhsh dipped his pen. He asked what the grandmother called her, what the weather had been on the day they last met, which of her sayings the girl still repeated. Then he began to write, slowly, leaving space at the bottom of the page, as he always did, for whatever the girl had not yet thought to say.

explanation: The passage shows Rahim Bakhsh losing customers to phones and then being sought out by a young woman who could text but wants his style. The nephew's offer is mentioned, but he is still at his table writing at the end.

stem: According to the passage, Rahim Bakhsh put the request for forgiveness at the end of the farmer's letter so that

explanation: The second paragraph says he wrote it last, in a single sentence, so that the brother could pretend not to have noticed it if he chose. Placing it last makes it easy to pass over, the opposite of making sure it is read first.

explanation: She says she could send a message in a second but wants the grandmother to hear it "the way you write", "Properly", which points to the quality of the words, not the medium. Nothing suggests the neighbour cannot read a phone; the passage says she reads out whatever comes.

stem: The detail that Rahim Bakhsh leaves "space at the bottom of the page" mainly suggests that he
options: has run short of the blue airmail paper he usually writes on.

explanation: The space is for "whatever the girl had not yet thought to say", echoing his early lesson that customers rarely know at first what they want to say. Nothing in the passage connects the space to his own advice or to payment.

title: The Karez of Balochistan
text:
In the dry valleys of Balochistan, rain is scarce and rivers are few, yet for centuries villages there have watered orchards and wheat fields from a source that is invisible from the surface. It flows through the karez, an underground channel that carries groundwater from the foot of the hills to the fields below. Seen from the air, a karez looks like a dotted line of small craters running across the plain: each crater is the mouth of a vertical shaft, and the shafts are linked at the bottom by a gently sloping tunnel.

The idea is simple, though building one is not. At the upper end, near the mountains, diggers sink a mother well until they reach the water table. From there they dig a tunnel back towards the village, sloping it so slightly that water flows along it by gravity alone, neither stagnating nor running fast enough to wear away the walls. The vertical shafts, spaced along the route, let diggers remove soil and let in air, and they remain as access points for cleaning. Where the tunnel finally reaches the surface, water emerges into an open channel and is shared among the fields.

The karez has two great advantages. Because the water travels underground, little is lost to evaporation, even in summer heat. And because it is drawn by gravity rather than pumped, it costs nothing to run. Its flow, however, depends on the level of groundwater, and it can deliver no more than the natural supply provides.

That limit became a weakness from the 1970s onward, as electric and diesel tube wells spread across the province. A tube well can pump water from far deeper than any karez reaches, and farmers who installed them could expand their fields quickly. But as pumping lowered the water table, many karez ran dry, and the communities that depended on them lost water they had shared for generations. The karez had also come with a social system: water was divided by turns measured in hours, and the families who held shares worked together to clean and repair the channel. When the karez failed, that system often failed with it.

Some villages have since begun to restore their channels. Whether they succeed may depend less on digging than on whether neighbours agree to pump less.

options: why Balochistan receives less rain than other provinces.
how electric tube wells are built and kept running by farmers.
how the karez works and why many of them have declined.
the history of wheat farming in the valleys of Balochistan.
explanation: The passage explains the karez's construction and advantages, then how tube wells lowered the water table and dried many of them up. Rainfall and tube-well construction are background details, not the subject.

explanation: The second paragraph says the shafts let diggers remove soil and let in air, and later serve as access points for cleaning. The karez works by gravity, so nothing in it is pumped.

stem: Based on the passage, a karez is most likely to keep flowing in a valley where
options: the tunnel is dug at a steep slope so that the water flows faster.

farmers draw little water from wells that reach deeper than the channel.
explanation: A karez can deliver only what the groundwater provides, and deep pumping lowered the water table and dried many up, so little deep pumping protects its flow. A steep slope would make the water run fast enough to wear away the walls, which the builders avoid.

stem: The final sentence of the passage suggests that restoring a karez depends partly on
options: neighbours agreeing among themselves to limit pumping.
digging new tunnels deeper than the original ones.
replacing gravity flow with electric or diesel pumps.
finding new sources of rain in the nearby mountains.
explanation: The sentence says success may depend less on digging than on whether neighbours agree to pump less, because pumping is what lowered the water table. Adding pumps would worsen the problem the passage describes.

title: A Hilltop Measure of the Earth
text:
In the early eleventh century, the scholar Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, who had come to the Punjab in the train of Mahmud of Ghazni, climbed a hill near the fort of Nandana in the Salt Range and set out to measure the size of the Earth. Earlier astronomers had attempted the same task, most famously by comparing the angle of the sun at two distant places on the same day. That approach required travel over long distances and careful measurement at both ends, and its results were only as good as the measured distance between the two places. Al-Biruni devised a method that could be carried out from a single spot.

His reasoning depended on geometry and on the plain below the hill. First he found the height of the hill itself, sighting its top from two points on the ground and working out the height from the angles. Then, standing on the summit, he measured how far the horizon dipped below the horizontal. On a flat Earth there would be no dip at all; on a curved one, the higher the observer, the further below the horizontal the horizon appears. Knowing the height of the hill and the angle of dip, he could treat the observer, the horizon and the centre of the Earth as the corners of a right-angled triangle and solve for the Earth's radius.

The answer he reached was remarkably close to the modern figure, within about one per cent by most calculations. Historians have pointed out that some of that accuracy may be luck: the dip angle at Nandana is small, a fraction of a degree, and the bending of light by the atmosphere affects where the horizon appears. A tiny error in measuring the angle could change the result considerably.

Yet the importance of the measurement does not depend on its exactness. What al-Biruni showed was that a question about the whole planet could be answered from one hilltop by a single observer with a sound argument and simple instruments. The method made the Earth's size a problem of reasoning rather than of travel, and that change in approach is what makes his visit to Nandana worth remembering.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Al-Biruni's result was more accurate than any modern measurement of the radius of the Earth.
Earlier astronomers proved that the Earth was curved by travelling across the Salt Range.
Al-Biruni's measurement was worthless, since the dip angle he relied on was so very small.
Al-Biruni's method mattered because it let one observer answer a question about the whole planet.
explanation: The final paragraph says the measurement's importance lies in turning the Earth's size into a problem of reasoning that one observer could solve from a hilltop. The small dip angle is raised as a source of possible error, but the author explicitly says the importance does not depend on exactness.

stem: According to the passage, what did al-Biruni measure while standing on the summit?
options: How far the horizon dipped below the horizontal
The angle of the sun at noon on that same day
The distance from the hill to the fort of Nandana
The height of the hill above the plain below it
explanation: The second paragraph says that on the summit he measured the dip of the horizon. He found the hill's height earlier, by sighting its top from two points on the ground.

stem: Based on the passage, al-Biruni's method would give no useful result if the observer
options: carried out the measurement alone, without any helpers.
found the hill's height by sighting it from two points.
used simple instruments rather than elaborate ones.
stood on ground no higher than the surrounding plain.
explanation: The dip of the horizon grows with the observer's height, so at no height above the plain there would be no measurable dip and nothing to solve for. The passage stresses that a single observer with simple instruments was enough.

stem: The third paragraph mainly serves to
options: show that al-Biruni deliberately altered his figure to agree with earlier ones.
temper praise for the result by noting how small errors could have affected it.

suggest that the modern figure for the Earth's radius is less reliable than his.
explanation: After calling the result remarkably close, the paragraph notes that a small dip angle and atmospheric bending mean some of the accuracy may be luck. It mentions the atmosphere's effect only briefly, as one reason for caution, without explaining it in detail.

title: Barcelona's Superblocks
text:
When the engineer Ildefons Cerdà designed the expansion of Barcelona in the 1850s, he laid out a grid of identical square blocks with cut-off corners, intended to bring light, air and movement to a crowded medieval city. A century and a half later, the grid he drew had become a grid of traffic. Almost every street in the Eixample district carried cars, and the city's planners faced a familiar modern problem: residents wanted quieter, cleaner streets, but the city could not simply close its roads.

Their answer, tried first in the Poblenou district in 2016, was the superilla, or superblock. Planners grouped nine blocks, three by three, into a single unit. Through traffic was kept to the roads around the outside of the unit, while the streets inside were opened only to residents' vehicles, deliveries and emergency services, at walking speed. Freed from most cars, the interior intersections were turned into small squares with benches, trees and play areas.

The appeal of the idea lies in what it does not require. No buildings were demolished and no new roads were built; the change was made largely with paint, planters and signs, so it was cheap and could be reversed if it failed. Supporters pointed to studies suggesting that superblocks across the city could, in time, cut air pollution and noise substantially and prevent a measurable number of early deaths.

The early reception was not warm. Some residents of Poblenou complained that they had not been consulted, and shopkeepers feared that customers who could no longer drive to their doors would go elsewhere. Drivers grumbled about longer routes. Over the following years, however, many objections softened as the squares filled with people, and the city extended the approach to other districts, this time with more public consultation before the paint went down.

Critics still raise a serious concern: traffic removed from the interior streets has to go somewhere, and the roads around the edges may become busier. A superblock, in other words, may make its own streets better partly by making its neighbours' worse. Whether the benefits outweigh this cost depends on whether, over time, people simply drive less.

stem: The passage mainly

explains why Barcelona's medieval streets were too narrow for modern traffic.
describes the superblock idea, how it was received and a doubt that remains.
compares Barcelona's superblocks with similar schemes in several other cities.
explanation: The passage explains how superblocks work, traces the move from early complaints to wider adoption, and ends with the concern about traffic pushed to the edges. It keeps Cerdà's grid and adapts it, and it mentions no other cities.

explanation: The second paragraph lists residents' vehicles, deliveries and emergency services, all at walking speed. Walking speed is a condition on those vehicles, not permission for any vehicle, since through traffic is kept to the outer roads.

explanation: The fourth paragraph says the city extended the approach "this time with more public consultation", answering Poblenou residents' complaint that they had not been consulted. Nothing suggests the method changed to demolition or permanent works.

explanation: The next sentence explains the phrase: no buildings were demolished and no new roads built, so the scheme was cheap and reversible. The lack of consultation was a drawback raised by critics, not part of the idea's appeal.
